                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Public explanations of flooding in Greater Accra frequently foreground indiscriminate waste disposal. This study aims to argue that such behaviour matters but becomes analytically misleading when separated from the institutions that organise land development, drainage, wetlands and the waste chain. Its main objective is to explain how landfill governance and land-use institutions mediate the relationship between waste and flood-risk production in Greater Accra.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>It combines a critical interpretive synthesis, qualitative document analysis and secondary satellite change detection around Kpone, Adekopa–Sonitra and the western corridor. Urban political ecology explains how flood exposure is produced through uneven urbanisation, while the Institutional Analysis and Development framework identifies how authority mismatch, information gaps, monitoring failures and weak sanctioning sustain that exposure.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Six classified maps achieved 86.4%–99.5% internal hold-out accuracy (kappa = 0.80–0.99). Only the western corridor produced change exceeding the combined classification-error allowance where built-up land increased by 3.59 km⁲ between 2006 and 2026.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The article’s theoretical contribution is the governance-mediated urban-risk cascade, which links landfill lifecycle pressures, infrastructure disruption and spatial redistribution of exposure.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings support transparent facility information, ring-fenced closure finance, emergency waste-routeing plans, interoperable spatial records and long-term environmental monitoring.</jats:p>

title: Using Cobalt and Molybdenum for improve productivity and seed quality of some soybean genotypes

items.abstract: <jats:p>This study aimed to enhance the physiological and agronomic performance of three elite soybean genotypes (H18L54, Masry 10, and Giza 111) through the application of Cobalt and Molybdenum each at concentration of 50 ppm, either as seed priming treatment or foliar sprays applied at 30 and 45 days after sowing during 2023 and 2024 growing seasons. Field experiments were conducted using a randomized complete block design arranged in a split- plot design with three replications Laboratory assessment of seed germination and seedling vigor performed using a completely randomized design with four replications. Field results demonstrated that agronomic and quality traits including plant height, 100-seed weight, number of pods per plant, seed oil content, seed yield per feddan, and days to 50% flowering were significantly affected by the main effects of genotype and treatment. However, genotype x treatment (G×T) interactions were generally non-significant under field environments. Genotype Giza 111 exhibited exceptional yield potential (2,571.1 kg/fed) and plant height (103.3 cm), whereas Masry 10 produced the highest seed index (100-seed weight of 18.5 g), demonstrating strong genetic determination of seed size. Seed priming with Cobalt (50 ppm) proved highly effective in boosting early seedling physiological vigor, significantly accelerating speed germination, seedling length, and dry biomass accumulation under controlled laboratory conditions, accompanied by significant G×T interaction effects. Foliar applications displayed moderate efficacy compared to seed priming treatments. Hence, seed priming technique with Cobalt and Molybdenum represents a highly cost-effective and physiological-efficient strategy, early seedling vigor, and maximum seed yield in soybean production systems.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>To quantify the carbon footprint (CF) of dairy farms, numerous studies and calculators have been developed to determine greenhouse gas emissions. However, methodological variations across studies frequently lead to inconsistent or non-comparable results. This study evaluated the greenhouse gas emissions of dairy production using a two-farm case study design of two specific Portuguese dairy farms: a conventional intensive farm (Case A) and a pasture-based organic farm (Case B). The IPCC methodology was applied to estimate greenhouse gas emissions associated with ruminal fermentation, manure storage and nitrogen application to soils. The Rothamsted carbon model was used to estimate the amount of carbon sequestered in the soil of natural pastures on the organic farm. Our results show a carbon footprint of 1.43 kg of CO2-eq/kg of energy-corrected milk (ECM) for the conventional farm and 2.82 kg of CO2-eq/kg of ECM for the organic farm. When considering soil carbon sequestration in natural pastures, the CF of the organic farm was reduced to 2.06 kg of CO2-eq/kg of ECM. Feed import was the largest source of emissions on the conventional farm, whereas ruminal fermentation was the largest source on the organic farm. Because this analysis is structured as a two-farm case study, the results represent the specific conditions of these two individual cases and are not generalize to conventional and organic dairy production systems as a whole. Nevertheless, this study constitutes a useful empirical baseline for identifying targeted greenhouse gas mitigation measures on these two farms—such as culling unproductive animals, adjusting diets, and improving effluent management—while highlighting the role of animal productivity in reducing emissions per liter of milk, as well as the impact of carbon sequestration in natural pastures on the carbon footprint.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As geopolitical shifts reshape global sourcing, firms increasingly reconsider suppliers in regions previously excluded by sanctions, boycotts and other geopolitical instruments. Such exclusions often leave a lasting stigma, and suppliers in these regions struggle to establish legitimacy as buyers discount their signals. This research examines how supply chain intermediaries undertake legitimation work to overcome suppliers' legitimacy deficits that otherwise deter reintegration.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conduct a longitudinal multiple-case study in the Uzbekistan cotton–textile industry (2019–2026), a revelatory instance of reintegration after the lifting of a global boycott. The three cases are buyer–supplier relationships in this setting, each brokered by the same three intermediaries. We draw abductively on 46 interviews with buyers, suppliers and intermediaries, over 80 h of observations, and 2,231 pages of archival documents.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Uzbek suppliers face three legitimacy deficits: cognitive illegibility, pragmatic incompatibility and moral fragility. In response, intermediaries employ three strategies: (1) cognitive bridging to render suppliers comprehensible; (2) network grafting to make exchange workable; and (3) norm cascading to embed global standards into supplier practices so that compliance becomes credible and durable. Together, these strategies move suppliers from exclusion to accepted sourcing relationships with global buyers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We extend supply chain geopolitics research to reintegration, showing how a previously excluded region re-enters global sourcing following a geopolitical shift. We theorize intermediated legitimation as the mechanism enabling this, with legitimation work shifting to the intermediary. Contrary to the sequence assumed in prior literature, cognitive legitimacy emerges as the gateway to pragmatic and moral legitimacy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Generating entangled photons from a laser-driven spin provides a promising resource for quantum communication, but their usefulness can depend on how the surrounding nuclear environment evolves during photon generation. We investigate a spin–photon interface driven by finite laser pulses while retaining nuclear-spin dynamics across successive emission cycles. Measurements on the intermediate photons produce conditional endpoint states, whose entanglement, Bell correlations, teleportation fidelity, and expected detection rates are evaluated. By comparing dynamically evolving, frozen-field, and reset nuclear environments, we find that simplified noise models can predict different operating windows for useful teleportation. In particular, the frozen-field approximation may overestimate performance under the conditions studied. Optical branching, imperfect feedforward, and nuclear-register size further constrain these windows. The results establish a task-oriented framework for evaluating photonic resources while highlighting the need for accurate environmental modeling and device-specific calibration.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) cost models are typically built around the build phase alone, omitting pre-and post-processing activities that account for a high share of the total manufacturing cost. This paper presents a dynamic Time-Driven Activity-Based Costing (TDABC) approach that decomposes the LPBF process chain into discrete activities and identifies the cost driver governing each one. An Activity-Resource-Data (ARD) mapping procedure was used to assign each activity its primary cost driver, a real-time data source, and a sustainability indicator. This approach accommodates variability through part-specific time equations that activate only the activities a given job requires thus charging only resources consumed. Since cost drivers and environmental metrics share the same operational engine, the carbon footprint and powder recycling efficiency were derived simultaneously from a single data stream, thereby establishing a formal cost-carbon-recycling nexus. A stochastic layer propagates key input uncertainties, such as printing time, powder yield, and labour duration uncertainty through all equations simultaneously, yielding confidence intervals which support robust lifecycle costing. The approach provides a traceable, auditable foundation for integrated economic and environmental analysis within a LPBF process chain.</jats:p>

                  <jats:p>We report the design, fabrication, and performance of a kilogram-scale, laser-driven annular photoreactor for preparative photochemistry. Building on a previously reported 0.5 W light-diffusing-fiber (LDF) prototype, we increased reactor volume ∼8× and scaled delivered optical power by ∼1600× by employing a different LDF and an 800 W diode laser. Externalizing photon generation keeps electrical and heat-generating components remote from hazardous chemical environments, facilitating the use in ATEX-rated facilities, and enables full enclosure of the emitted light for improved operational safety. The prototype was evaluated on a nickel-catalyzed C–N cross-coupling, delivering high, reproducible conversions across a range of flow rates, optical powers, and photocatalyst concentrations. Compared with a benchmark LED-driven tubular photoreactor, the present design increased the efficiency of delivered photon utilization within the reactor volume by ∼3×. A mechanistic PDE model was applied to accurately predict conversion across the ∼1600× scale-up in laser power (parity R2 = 0.981). These results indicate that laser-driven annular photoreactors offer a safe, controllable, and scalable platform capable of a model-projected multikilogram-per-day photochemical production suitable for small-molecule pharmaceutical manufacturing.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>It is widely recognized that low-level laser irradiation affects immune system cells in various ways, one of which is enhancing the phagocytic activity of the treated cells. <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>A sigma-cavity laser configuration, consisting of ring and linear sections, is known to provide stable single-frequency (SF) generation. However, using an Er-doped fiber laser as an example we demonstrate that in addition to typical stable SF generation self-sweeping can occur even with moderate isolation of ∼37 dB provided in the ring section by a standard circulator. We demonstrate that the generation regime—SF stabilization, self-sweeping, or multi-frequency operation—can be controlled by introducing additional losses in the laser cavity. Depending on the specific point of the cavity where the losses are introduced, the sweeping rate can either increase or decrease with attenuation variation. The observed regimes are explained in terms of an extremely weak counter-propagating wave forming gain dynamic population grating in the ring section of the cavity. The results provide new insights into mode dynamics in sigma-cavity fiber lasers. They can be of use both for the task of mode-hopping suppression required for stable SF operation and for the task of controlling the self-sweeping rate for applications requiring wavelength tuning.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We study the dependence of neutron‐star scalar fields on high‐density equations of state (EoSs) in linearly coupled Einstein–dilaton–Gauss–Bonnet gravity in the decoupling approximation. For five GM1L models and SW4L, we solve the scalar equation on fixed general‐relativistic stellar backgrounds. The surface scalar field is more tightly grouped when plotted against compactness than against mass, although EoS‐dependent offsets remain. An analytic Schwarzschild‐exterior solution with vanishing scalar monopole charge shows that the surface field is fixed by the stellar mass and radius; its nonmonotonic variation along each sequence reflects the competing changes in compactness and mass along the EoS‐dependent mass–radius relation. Numerical tests support outer‐boundary convergence, vanishing asymptotic monopole charge, and the expected linear scaling with coupling strength. The EoS dependence of the surface scalar field is therefore encoded in the stellar mass–radius relation, whereas the interior scalar profile retains sensitivity to the detailed matter distribution. These results provide a baseline for assessing how uncertainties in the high‐density EoS may influence scalar‐field signatures in more general scalar–Gauss–Bonnet theories.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Laser Metal Deposition (LMD) is a laser-based additive manufacturing process used for the deposition of metallic materials and composites. The resulting microstructure and properties are influenced by processing conditions and material composition. This study investigates the combined influence of TiC reinforcement content and laser power on the microstructural characteristics and microhardness of commercially pure titanium (CpTi)/TiC composites deposited on Ti6Al4V substrates. Powder mixtures containing 10–40 wt.% TiC were deposited using a Yb-fibre LMD system at laser powers of 0.8 and 1.6 kW. The deposited composites were characterised using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and Vickers microhardness testing. SEM observations revealed differences in the distribution of dispersed features, localised pore-like features, and acicular α/α′-type morphologies within the deposited layers under the investigated processing conditions. The deposited layers exhibited continuous deposit–substrate interfaces in the examined cross-sections, providing qualitative evidence of interfacial continuity. The Ti6Al4V substrate exhibited an average microhardness of 383 HV₀.₁, while the deposited composites exhibited microhardness values ranging from 364 to 460 HV₀.₁. The highest microhardness of 460 HV₀.₁ was obtained for the composite containing 40 wt.% TiC deposited at 1.6 kW. The results indicate that laser power and TiC reinforcement content jointly influence the microstructural characteristics and microhardness of LMD-produced CpTi/TiC composites.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Unidimensional-modulation (UD) continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) has emerged as a promising approach to quantum-secure access networks because it requires comparatively simple and inexpensive hardware. Nevertheless, the resilience of multi-user UD CV-QKD systems to side-channel attacks has not been comprehensively investigated. This study proposes a multi-port distributed injection attacks model adapted to real deployment scenarios. A comprehensive theoretical model of the attack in broadcast architectures is established, and the asymptotic secret key rate is derived under the worst-case assumption that an eavesdropper controls all non-target users. The results demonstrate that the attack biases system parameter estimation, thereby causing overestimation of the secret key rate, and that the multi-user passive optical architecture intrinsically exacerbates this security threat. Furthermore, the analysis is extended to the practical finite-size regime and identifies a critical vulnerability, whereby the attack can induce the system to generate spurious secure keys even when the sample size is inadequate to yield any valid keys in the corresponding attack-free scenario. These findings demonstrate that the multi-port distributed injection attacks pose a significant practical security risk to real-world multi-user UD CV-QKD deployments, and offers valuable theoretical guidance for the security design of quantum-secure access networks.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Laser-induced graphene (LIG) provides a scalable, maskless route to porous carbon electrodes, but variability among independently fabricated devices and batches limits reliable manufacturing. Here, a controlled Ag/LIG workflow was used to examine how a one- to three-pass laser sequence affects material structure, electrochemical response, and fabrication reproducibility. SEM indicated pass-dependent network restructuring within the sampled fields, Raman spectroscopy showed greater but spatially nonuniform graphitic ordering, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy indicated greater sp2 character and modest surface deoxygenation with repeated laser exposure. Three-pass electrodes produced an approximately 2.3-fold higher square-wave voltammetric response than one-pass electrodes in ferri/ferrocyanide solution. Cyclic voltammetry, impedance spectroscopy, and direct resistance measurements on representative electrodes showed that the largest resistance decrease occurred between one and two passes, whereas conditional apparent electroactive area continued to increase, with the larger increment occurring between two and three passes; charge-transfer resistance remained comparatively small and showed no systematic dependence on pass number. Reproducibility of the selected three-pass process was evaluated using 18 devices from three fabrication batches and 162 voltammograms: scan-to-scan relative SD was below 0.5%, while device-within-batch and batch relative SDs were 2.6–3.6% and 2.0–4.4%, respectively. These results link controlled multipass processing to staged improvements in electrical transport and electrochemical accessibility and provide a hierarchical framework for quantifying the fabrication reproducibility of porous carbon electrodes.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Accurate intraoperative identification of tumor boundaries remains a major challenge in surgical oncology, particularly for infiltrative tumors, anatomically constrained lesions, and cancers adjacent to critical vessels, nerves, or functional tissues. Conventional visual inspection, palpation, and preoperative imaging may provide insufficient or outdated information once tissue deformation and surgical manipulation occur. Optical methods can provide real‐time structural, molecular, metabolic, and functional contrast across multiple spatial scales, supporting tumor localization, subsurface margin assessment, localized tissue characterization, and preservation of critical anatomy. This review examines intraoperative optical guidance from a decision‐oriented perspective, organizing current technologies according to the surgical questions they are best positioned to address, from wide‐field localization to depth‐resolved assessment and microscopic or molecular characterization. By comparing the complementary strengths and limitations of these approaches across spatial scales, this review highlights how optical guidance may be tailored to different intraoperative decisions, while also identifying the technical and clinical barriers that continue to limit broader translation.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Above the Hoyle resonance, the excited states of the 12C nucleus begin to overlap strongly. To separate them, various theoretical models are used, which predict different spectra of angular distributions of the decay products (α-particles). This leads to discrepancies of   or more in cross-section estimates in the ENDF, JEFF, and JENDL nuclear databases.  In this work, we investigate the hypothesis of a possible connection between the population of resonant states of the 12C  nucleus and the scattering of a projectile neutron on various clusters of the 12C  nucleus with a  3α or α –8Be structure. For this purpose, the interaction of 14 MeV neutrons with a stationary 12C nucleus was investigated, where within a nuclear potential well of depth 45 MeV and width  L ∼ 5 fm, the de Broglie wavelength of the incident neutron (λ n ≈ 0.58 fm) allows it to spatially resolve intranuclear  clusters (λα ∼ 1.68 fm). Therefore, as a first rough approximation, independent quantum scattering of a neutron off the 12C nuclear clusters is modeled in momentum-energy representation, leading to nuclear excitation. To this end, the partial differential cross sections for nα and n – 8Be scattering were adopted from the phenomenological phase-shift analysis by Tilleessen et al. (IAEA EXFOR Database). Monte Carlo simulations allowed us to calculate the mass-energy distribution of the excited 12C* nucleus and make a comparison with experimental population probabilities for the excited 12C*. Despite the rough approximation of cluster independence, qualitative consistency is observed. A strong discrepancy occurs at points where strict quantum suppression or nuclear collectivity is strongly dominant. For neutron scattering on different cluster structures, the model predicts different population probabilities for the excited 12C*, which indicates the need for further calculations within a more realistic model that strictly accounts for the overlap of the de Broglie waves of the α-particles.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Photonic time crystals are spatially uniform media whose material parameters vary periodically in time, opening momentum bandgaps within which the fields of electromagnetic modes can grow exponentially in time. To date, most studies on such crystals have utilized only passive materials with “positive” dispersion (satisfying Foster's reactance theorem). Here we propose a theoretical framework of photonic time crystals based on active materials with “negative” dispersion (non‐Foster materials). We explore two representative classes of isotropic non‐Foster photonic time crystals: a bulk medium with time‐modulated effective permittivity and a metasurface whose surface capacitance is switched in time. We show that an ideal lossless and dispersionless non‐Foster model can produce exceptionally broad momentum bandgaps, with amplification rates increase approximately linearly with momentum and the ability to amplify direct‐current (DC) waves. To move beyond this idealized limit, we further introduce a causal finite‐bandwidth Lorentz/inverted‐Lorentz model. Similar results are found in this model but with truncated bandgaps and conditional DC amplification. These results extend the theory of photonic time crystals to active non‐Foster reactive responses, providing a route to Floquet engineering and a more complete understanding of wave–matter interactions in time‐varying media.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Intravenous (IV) fluid contamination is a common cause of misleading laboratory results. Machine learning approaches may complement fixed rules, delta checks, and manual review, but developing and validating models requires technical expertise that has limited widespread adoption.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>FluidFlagger is an open-source application that packages a model-development and evaluation work flow for contamination detection behind a browser-based interface that requires no programming knowledge. Pretrained models were evaluated retrospectively against focused expert-adjudication labels in held-out basic metabolic panel (BMP) and complete blood count (CBC) subsets (127 and 37 labeled contaminated specimens, respectively) and against previously optimized comparator model outputs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>BMP classifiers discriminated contamination with areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (auROCs) of 0.974 (real-time) and 0.969 (retrospective); CBC classifiers achieved 0.763 and 0.879. Specificity exceeded 97% for all models, whereas sensitivity was variable, reflecting a predominance of mild contamination events and the need for local threshold calibration.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>FluidFlagger provides an accessible framework for training and validating institution-specific models for detecting IV fluid contamination, lowering the barrier to local evaluation across laboratories of varying informatics expertise. Prospective clinical use requires local integration, threshold evaluation, validation, governance, and monitoring.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Political discourse spans institutions, languages and historical periods, yet the archives preserving it often remain fragmented and difficult to compare. This paper introduces the Indian Political Text Corpus (IPTC) v1.1, a source-linked resource comprising 75,431 records and 524,473,982 whitespace-delimited words from Indian executive, party and parliamentary archives, principally covering 2004–2026. Integrating English, Hindi and mixed-language materials, IPTC preserves institutional provenance, documentary genres, archival language labels and source-specific quality information within a common analytical framework. We describe its compilation, metadata architecture and validation procedures, demonstrating an approach to organising heterogeneous political archives while documenting extraction limitations and historical encoding conditions. Beyond its scale, IPTC provides a foundation for examining how political authority is articulated across institutions, how collective identities and social boundaries are constructed through political discourse, and how political agendas and institutional narratives evolve over time. These applications connect corpus-assisted linguistic analysis with questions in political science, sociology and political communication. By linking textual evidence to its institutional and documentary contexts, IPTC supports comparative, multilingual and diachronic research on political language in contemporary India.</jats:p>

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study presents a conceptual framework for continuously detecting, scoring and correcting enterprise knowledge gaps with large language models (LLMs). The framework operationalizes knowledge degradation through a multidimensional Knowledge Article Quality Index (AQI) defined across six dimensions: accuracy, completeness, actionability, freshness, discoverability and outcome effectiveness. The AQI operates within a closed-loop governance architecture designed to preserve knowledge integrity at enterprise scale.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper develops a conceptual framework informed by design-science principles for continuous enterprise knowledge governance. The framework integrates a multidimensional AQI, evidence-grounded LLM-based semantic assessment, separate behavioral telemetry, degradation detection and governance-controlled remediation. The conceptual design is derived by linking theoretical constructs from knowledge entropy, socio-technical systems and information quality to explicit design principles and operational mechanisms. The proposed architecture and evaluation criteria are specified for future demonstration and empirical validation rather than presented as empirically validated results.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The framework specifies a closed-loop mechanism through which enterprise knowledge artifacts can be assessed, monitored, flagged for potential degradation and routed for governance-controlled remediation. Three design propositions are formulated to guide future empirical evaluation: (DP1) integrating evidence-grounded semantic assessment with independent behavioral telemetry is expected to support earlier identification of potential knowledge degradation than periodic manual review, (DP2) governance-controlled remediation is expected to increase AQI and reduce the AQI deficit and (DP3) governance-controlled automation is expected to support improved knowledge-related operational outcomes. These propositions are theoretical expectations rather than empirically demonstrated findings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The framework provides a governance-oriented architecture for continuously monitoring enterprise knowledge quality and identifying potential knowledge gaps. It specifies how semantic assessment, behavioral telemetry and controlled remediation can be integrated while retaining human oversight and auditability. Potential improvements in containment, escalation management and resolution efficiency are treated as future evaluation outcomes rather than demonstrated effects. The framework is particularly relevant to enterprise environments in which knowledge accuracy, traceability, compliance and controlled AI-assisted correction are important.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study introduces the LLM-Driven Knowledge AQI Remediation Loop, which reconceptualizes enterprise knowledge management as a continuously monitored, governance-controlled system. Its originality lies in integrating established knowledge-quality, LLM-evaluation, behavioral-telemetry and governance mechanisms into a unified architecture, rather than in the weighted AQI formula itself. By treating the AQI as a state variable, separating content-based assessment from behavioral telemetry and embedding remediation within governance controls, the paper advances conceptual and architectural approaches to AI-enabled knowledge governance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Consolidating deliveries to fuel stations requires balancing fewer joint orders against inventory levels and demand fulfillment. This study proposes an adaptive can-order policy in which Random Forest periodically selects the intensity of a dynamic adjustment to the threshold for including items in joint orders. Three main policies are compared: a static baseline, full adaptation, and adaptation with data-driven intensity selection. Experiments use 444 real daily demand series, three fuels, 864 configurations, and 20 random station partitions. Validation covers days 181–365, starting at order-up-to levels without outstanding deliveries and carrying states across six consecutive periods. The proposed policy averages 12.23% delivery reduction and 1.99% inventory growth versus baseline, with fill rate virtually unchanged. After full-horizon aggregation, approximately 62% of configurations meet the compromise criterion, versus 21% under full adaptation. The compromise share reflects compliance with the adopted tolerances, which permit unchanged delivery counts. Consolidation benefits are greatest at low and moderate baseline can-order thresholds. Compared with the low fixed adaptation intensity, the proposed policy achieves greater delivery savings with higher inventory growth and a lower compromise share. The intermediate and high fixed adaptation intensities achieve greater delivery savings, with higher inventory growth and lower compromise shares than the proposed policy.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Energy and exergy analyses of a geothermal-driven Organic Rankine Cycle (ORC) utilizing alternative organic mixtures with low global warming potential (GWP) as working fluids were conducted. New mixtures were created in REFPROP 10 using organic fluids commonly employed in fluid analysis. Among the 108 newly formulated organic working fluid mixtures, 12 candidates characterized by a temperature glide of less than 5 °C, a high critical temperature, and a GWP value below 750 were selected for this study. Energy and exergy assessments were performed for power generation using the selected fluids at geothermal brine temperatures of 130–150 °C (in 5 °C increments) and a condenser temperature of 30 °C. Additionally, the cycle’s net power output (W˙net), thermal efficiency (ηth) and second-law efficiency (ηıı) were quantified. Based on the simultaneous maximization of W˙net, ηth and ηıı specific fluid recommendations are proposed: b7 is optimal for low-temperature, ultra-low-GWP geothermal and waste heat conversation (GWP < 150, TCR < 165 °C); b1 is recommended for high-enthalpy geothermal applications requiring low environmental impact (GWP < 150, TCR > 165 °C); and b9 serves as the prime candidate for medium-GWP (150 < GWP < 750) commercial power plants aiming for maximum energy conversation. Among all evaluated working fluids, b7 (GWP < 150) achieved the maximum W˙net, ηth and ηii, proving to be the most promising organic blend owing to its favorable thermophysical properties and ultra-low GWP.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>With the rapid advancements in experimental techniques and the growth in the amount of available data, especially when using digital image correlation and tomography, modelling is facing the challenge of transforming this enormous amount of knowledge into analytical equations that govern the material response. Classical constitutive equations may struggle to meet such a challenge, which is among the reasons why data-driven approaches emerged. In this study, we apply a data-driven scheme to the modelling of failure of a quasi-brittle (strain-softening) material and discuss the difficulties induced when modelling localized failure. For the sake of simplicity, we consider a one-dimensional problem. Synthetic data sets are generated from a bi-linear damage model and with a mesoscale model representative of concrete. As expected, the one-dimensional example of a bar subjected to tension demonstrates that the obtained solutions are sensitive to the finite element discretization. A localization limiter is needed and the implementation of a non-local (integral) model may be expected to circumvent this difficulty. There is, however, a notable challenge because the minimization problem requires an enhancement that accounts for non-local interactions, which is non trivial and may yield ill-posedness. The Lip-field formulation provides a practical alternative to maintain the local nature of the data set and turns out to be easily implemented in this data-driven computational framework.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) in the field of photovoltaics (PV) has resulted in a fragmented, interdisciplinary corpus of knowledge that obscures the connection between nanoscale phenomena and device performance and system reliability. The performance-determining processes of solar cells, including light absorption, charge separation, defect-mediated recombination, and interfacial degradation, occur at the atomic to nanometer scale. Consequently, this fragmentation is both a nanoscale problem and a computational problem. In this study, we present a comprehensive bibliometric and semantic synthesis of AI-PV research from 2015 to 2025. This synthesis maps the literature from the nanoscale to the system level by integrating established bibliometric tools with transformer-based topic modeling (BERTopic). A comprehensive analysis of 1,326 publications reveals a three-stage expansion, with 81.8 % of the cumulative output concentrated in the accelerated phase (2022–2025). The nine resulting topics are organized into an expert-defined, cross-scale taxonomy: (i) AI-guided discovery and atomic-scale engineering of absorber materials, lattices, and grain boundaries; (ii) physics-informed regulation of nanoscale transport layers, interfaces, and photonic nanostructures; and (iii) data-driven reliability assurance and system integration, where macroscopic failures are traced to their nanoscale origins. We also discuss how nonvalidated information can potentially bias expectations regarding the performance of devices. This synthesis identifies a shift from black-box efficiency prediction toward physics-constrained, multifidelity design and highlights nanoscale grain boundary dynamics and photonic metamaterials as pivotal frontiers.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>The increasing frequency and duration of droughts are contributing to the escalation of water scarcity in many regions globally, posing significant threats to the environmental, social, and economic sectors, and affecting their sustainability, operations, and development. Long-term, sustainable planning and management of water resources need to address the emergent challenges posed by more pronounced climate change impacts. The study explores the improved performance of a developed method of integrated hydro–climate modeling when implemented in synergy with a participatory process, as well as the enhancements achieved thereby, toward climate resilience of complex systems. The selected study area is the transboundary region of Ohrid and Prespa Lakes, explored during the Horizon 2020-funded project ARSINOE. The presented modeling method consists of three phases: 1) estimation of future water availability, 2) assessment of sectoral vulnerability, and 3) establishing climate adaptation strategies. Specific integration is applied in each phase, consistently taking into consideration the stakeholders' declared national and regional values and priorities. The main achievements include: identification of projected water scarcity and arising cross-sectoral trade-offs, a quantified indicators–based evaluation of impact, and selection of balanced adaptation strategies. The results feature recognized relevance across sectors, borders, and communities and provide advancements toward complex resilience, due to the integration method, comprehensiveness, and co-creation applied in the deployment of systemic innovative solutions, fostering transboundary collaboration in long-term water management.</jats:p>

title: How task complexity influences the impact of feedback source–content combinations on managerial performance: empirical evidence from a manufacturing case study

affiliation.name: University of Virginia’s College at Wise Department of Business and Economics, , Wise, ,

items.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper aims to develop actionable research by addressing three key questions: (1) Does performance feedback interact with task complexity to influence managerial performance? (2) How does supervisor leadership influence managerial performance in environments with high task complexity? and (3) Which feedback combinations are likely to be most beneficial to organizations under varying conditions of managerial task complexity?</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A seven-month, time-lagged 2 × 2 factorial field experiment analyzes the effects of feedback source (external performance coach vs internal human resource representative), feedback content (developmental vs goals) combinations and supervisory leadership on 265 managers, categorized by task complexity and evaluated based on changes in pre- and post-feedback performance scores.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>There are three key findings: (1) An external performance coach is likely to be more effective than an internal HR representative as a source of feedback, (2) the magnitude of the positive difference in impact between the external performance coach and the internal HR representative reduces under conditions of high task complexity and (3) the most effective feedback combination is an external performance coach providing developmental feedback.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The field experiment should be replicated across industries and business environments using longitudinal designs to improve generalizability and the actionability of its recommendations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings provide specific guidance on designing performance feedback interventions under varying task complexity conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The field experiment results challenge the conventional view of the effectiveness of external coaches and experts and suggest limits to their impact under high managerial task complexity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The field experiment is among the first to examine the effectiveness of various feedback combinations under conditions of managerial task complexity in a real-world organizational setting, providing actionable guidance and practical insights for feedback scholars and practitioners.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:italic>Purpose</jats:italic>
                    . A Geant4-based model was created to simulate radiation transport within a novel radiotherapy system developed by Convergent Radiotherapy and Radiosurgery (Convergent RnR; Haifa, Israel). This treatment device incorporates a Bragg-diffraction x-ray lens to focus x-rays from a conventional x-ray tube towards a small but finite focal spot with quasi-monoenergetic photons.
                    <jats:italic>Methods.</jats:italic>
                    The simulation model included an x-ray tube and a CRnR focusing lens consisting of single-crystal aluminum tiles. To validate the Geant4 model of this device, transverse and longitudinal in-air and in-water dose distributions from the converging beam field were calculated and compared to radiochromic film measurements.
                    <jats:italic>Results.</jats:italic>
                    The implemented Monte Carlo (MC) simulation model predicted a mean photon energy of 53.96 keV and showed agreement within 0.5% when compared with the SpekPy calculation. Both the simulation and experiment produced an attenuation characteristics of 3.2 mm Al. In-water tissue maximum ratios showed percentage differences ⩽3% at depths of 5, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, and 70 mm. Exceptions were observed at 80, and 85 mm, likely due to reduced film statistics, local dose variations, and positioning uncertainty. A gamma analysis of in-water scanning dose distributions demonstrated a >96% pass rate for the 2%/2 mm criterion and >99% for the 3%/3 mm criterion across all focal depths.
                    <jats:italic>Conclusions.</jats:italic>
                    In this study, CRnR’s converging beam radiotherapy system was implemented in Geant4 to demonstrate the device operation and characterize its physical and dosimetric outputs. The MC simulation implemented in this work successfully demonstrated converging dose distributions with Bragg-diffraction physics, which were in good agreement with radiochromic film measurements. This simulation model may be used to further refine the converging beam system design for clinical implementation, including validation of the treatment planning system.
                  </jats:p>

<jats:p>
                    Structural materials in nuclear reactors are susceptible to defect accumulation and embrittlement during prolonged irradiation, which can compromise reactor safety. To address the limitations of traditional approaches, including the lack of a temporal dimension in Monte Carlo simulations, the difficulty of directly linking molecular dynamics simulations to macroscopic mechanical analysis, and the neglect of irradiation-induced porosity in continuum models, this study proposes a multi-scaled failure prediction methodology. The Monte Carlo method based on binary collision approximation was used to quantify the irradiation damage dose (displacements per atom) of STC4 titanium alloy. Subsequently, the irradiation damage dose is converted into the porosity internal variable used in the Gurson–Tvergaard–Needleman (GTN) damage model. Through the coupled multi-scaled GTN damage model, the irradiation damage effects on the failure evolution and mechanical degradation are investigated and compared. At an incident energy of 200 keV and a fluence of 5 × 10
                    <jats:sup>15</jats:sup>
                    ions·cm
                    <jats:sup>−2</jats:sup>
                    , the simulations predict an approximately 13.27% increase in peak von Mises stress and a 39.1% reduction in maximum displacement relative to the unirradiated specimen. This framework examines how irradiation-induced defects affect the strength, ductility, and damage evolution of STC4 titanium alloy. The calibrated GTN model reproduces the unirradiated tensile response well, while the predicted irradiation-induced hardening and ductility degradation are consistent with previously reported experimental observations on irradiated titanium alloys. Direct quantitative validation under identical ion irradiation conditions is still required.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec id="S1460396926100703_as1">
                    <jats:title>Introduction:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Bilateral arm abduction remains the preferred standard for breast radiotherapy, but postoperative shoulder restrictions often necessitate alternative positioning. Building on the Bi-Arm study framework, this prospective pilot evaluation assessed a Novel Arm Support Device (NASD) designed for unilateral arm abduction, examining its feasibility, geometric setup reproducibility, patient experience and operational impact.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="S1460396926100703_as2">
                    <jats:title>Materials and methods:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Between September 2025 and May 2026, 15 NASD patients and 15 matched historical controls were enrolled, each cohort contributing 105 imaged fractions. Daily image-guided radiotherapy (IGRT) quantified population systematic (Σ) and random (σ) error data. Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), fraction-level repeat imaging rates and therapeutic radiographer surveys were evaluated against the historical control cohort.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="S1460396926100703_as3">
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The NASD demonstrated high clinical feasibility. Translational errors and 3D vector displacement (7·72 ± 3·12 mm vs. 7·21 ± 2·85 mm;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      = 0·334) broadly overlapped controls, while the NASD significantly stabilised systematic rotational pitch variations (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      = 0·046). PROMs yielded high patient acceptability, with median comfort scores of 4 (IQR: 4–5). At the fraction level, repeat imaging significantly decreased to 1·0% (1/105) for NASD versus 5·7% (6/105) for historical controls. Radiographers reported enhanced positioning consistency, with 87·5% reporting improved comfort and 14/16 demonstrating an overall preference for the NASD workflow.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="S1460396926100703_as4">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The NASD provides a practical, well-tolerated alternative that maintains geometric accuracy within standard tolerance frameworks for patients unable to tolerate bilateral positioning. Future research should prioritise a larger, multi-centre validation study with robust multivariable adjustments. Operationally, permanently dedicating an independent NASD assembly per active treatment room would optimise clinical workflows by eliminating inter-room scheduling delays.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

items.abstract: <jats:p>A self-consistent two-dimensional numerical model of an inductively coupled plasma (ICP) discharge in helium and He/SiH4 mixtures was developed to investigate the temporal evolution of charged and neutral species and the formation of a strongly electronegative plasma core. The model couples the RF electromagnetic field with plasma-chemical kinetics, charged-particle transport, electron energy balance, electrostatic potential, and gas heating. Particular attention was paid to the influence of negative-ion chemistry on the formation and evolution of the electronegative plasma core. Numerical simulations were performed using two alternative kinetic schemes: one including the formation of SiH4− and another excluding this channel while accounting for H− formation. The results demonstrate that a strongly electronegative central region develops in both kinetic schemes, although its formation time and spatial characteristics differ significantly. At an input power of 750 W and a pressure of 0.2 Torr, the maximum electronegativity reaches approximately 36.84 at 100 s when SiH4− formation is included, compared with 16.51 in the alternative model. The corresponding axial widths of the region satisfying α > 1 are approximately 1.97 and 1.56 cm, respectively. The accumulation of negative ions is accompanied by a pronounced redistribution of the self-consistent electric field and the formation of a broad low-field region in the discharge center. Analysis of neutral-species densities and estimated incident thermal fluxes reveals that atomic hydrogen and SiH are the dominant dissociation products of silane in both kinetic schemes, whereas SiH2, SiH3, and atomic silicon exhibit greater sensitivity to the adopted reaction mechanism. These findings demonstrate that the formation of a strongly electronegative plasma core is preserved under the investigated changes in negative-ion chemistry, while its quantitative characteristics and the relative availability of reactive species depend on the adopted kinetic scheme. The results provide insight into the formation and evolution of the electronegative plasma core and the production of reactive species under conditions relevant to silicon.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Meningioma is the most common primary intracranial tumor, and radiotherapy is central to managing higher-grade disease, yet PD-1 blockade has shown modest activity. We analyzed single-cell RNA sequencing of 11 xenografts of a single meningioma cell line (CH157-MN) that were unirradiated (n = 5) or sampled early (n = 3) or late (n = 3) after radiotherapy, pooling 77,827 human cells into pseudobulk profiles, and examined findings in two human bulk RNA-sequencing cohorts (n = 185 and n = 302). Radiotherapy induced interferon, chemokine, and antigen-presentation genes at the early timepoint. By the late timepoint, interferon effector and chemokine genes retained medians of 44% and 17% of their early induction, whereas CD274 (PD-L1) remained elevated above control (q = 0.041) without statistically detectable decline; relative to interferon effectors, CD274 rose 2.66 log2 units between timepoints (p = 0.009). In both human cohorts, checkpoint scores correlated with interferon scores (ρ = 0.48 and 0.65) and with a xenograft-derived radiation-priming signature (ρ = 0.61 and 0.76). In this model, the interferon program was transient, whereas CD274 declined less; these transcriptional findings do not establish functional immunosuppression and raise a hypothesis about the timing of PD-1 blockade that requires prospective evaluation.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Shielding performance inferred from attenuation or nominal thickness can misrepresent the response of a finite semiconductor detector. This study uses Geant4 to map energy deposited in a silicon sensor of dimensions 20 mm × 20 mm × 0.5 mm behind polyethylene (PE) and PE–aluminium (PE–Al) shields under controlled photon, electron, and proton fields. Event-level scoring separates primary survival, residual entry energy, shield-generated secondaries, and finite shield coverage. The proton response was strongly non-monotonic near range-out: effective suppression occurred between 8–9 mm PE at 30 MeV and between 20–25 mm PE at 50 MeV, in agreement with NIST PSTAR projected ranges. For photons, short shield-to-sensor gaps increased silicon energy deposition, consistent with enhanced acceptance of shield-generated secondaries. At the final 100 mm gap, adding 0.5 mm Al to 25 mm PE improved the photon-response reduction by 3.083 ± 0.558 percentage points under the reference physics list; the uncertainty is a two-sided 95% sampling confidence-interval half-width and excludes physics-model uncertainty. An XCOM narrow-beam calculation gave 1.01 percentage points of additional uncollided primary-photon number removal, a different observable that cannot be subtracted from the detector-response change to quantify a secondary contribution. A finite-size test further showed that oblique protons could traverse an edge-clipped path in a nominally thick shield. Within the discrete candidate set, 25 mm PE was the lowest-mass configuration with positive mean response reduction in all four benchmark fields. These results define transport and geometry regimes that should be checked before a shielding design is advanced to mission-specific modelling or experimental qualification.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>This study introduces the use of electromagnetic waves in the 0.2-terahertz (THz) region (wavelengths of 1.2–1.5 mm) for the decomposition of wood polymers. Specifically, monolignol derivatives and low-molecular-weight sugars were extracted from native wood sections of eucalyptus, cedar, and pine using THz-wave irradiation at 22–23 °C. The corresponding fragmentation reactions of lignocellulose proceeded without solvents and were promoted in the presence of iron (III) chloride as a Lewis acid. These findings were confirmed by liquid chromatography in combination with electrospray ionization mass spectrometry, nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, synchrotron radiation infrared microscopy, and thermal imaging observations. Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of THz-wave irradiation as a physicochemical approach for treating wood.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Terahertz (THz) integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) is emerging as a key enabler of sixth generation (6G) networks, and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are among its most challenging yet valuable host platforms. Over ground-to-UAV links, THz-ISAC payloads promise ultra-high-rate to backhaul and millimeter-level sensing within the stringent size, weight, and power budget of a hovering drone. Realizing this promise requires a coherent understanding of four tightly coupled pillars: the ground-to-UAV THz channel, beam management, the ISAC waveform and its transceiver realization, and system-level performance. This survey is organized around these four pillars. We first consolidate the propagation fundamentals of aerial THz links, including altitude-dependent molecular absorption and UAV-specific non-stationarity, together with the measurement and modeling literature that underpins them. We then review beam management, covering near-field beam-pattern transformation, alignment and tracking under misalignment, and wideband hybrid beamforming that combats beam squint with true-time-delay architectures. We next contrast the candidate ISAC waveforms — OTFS, DFT-s-OTFS with superimposed pilots, and SI-DFT-s-OFDM with flexible guard intervals — in terms of PAPR, power-amplifier efficiency, Doppler robustness, and sensing accuracy, and assess the transceiver hardware against the UAV payload envelope. Finally, we discuss system-level performance, including localization bounds, spectral efficiency, and sensing/vision-aided mobility management, along with use cases and open challenges. Throughout, quantitative claims are traced to their source documents and to the specific figures from which they stem.</jats:p>

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Carotid artery disease is an important long-term vascular concern in nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) survivors after radiotherapy. However, its angiographic characteristics, particularly as assessed by digital subtraction angiography (DSA), remain incompletely characterized in clinically selected patients.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this retrospective single-center study, NPC patients who underwent clinically indicated DSA were included. Symptomatic ischemic events were defined as transient ischemic attack or ischemic stroke within the anterior circulation territory within 6 months prior to DSA. Angiographic features of the internal carotid artery (ICA) and common carotid artery (CCA), including stenosis severity and distribution, were evaluated. Severe stenosis was defined as ≥70%.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      A total of 98 patients were included, comprising 56 symptomatic and 42 asymptomatic patients. Severe ICA stenosis was more frequent in symptomatic than asymptomatic patients (78.6% vs. 47.6%,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.002), whereas severe CCA stenosis and bilateral severe carotid system stenosis showed no statistically significant between-group differences. In the overall cohort, severe ICA stenosis was more frequent than severe CCA stenosis (65.3% vs. 36.7%; two-sided exact McNemar test,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>

                  <jats:sec id="S1460396926100727_as1">
                    <jats:title>Introduction:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study compared single-arc (SA) and dual-arc (DA) VMAT for localised prostate cancer using an integrated assessment of dosimetric, radiobiological, deliverability, complexity and anatomical factors and evaluated whether anatomy-based metrics (Mq,r index and F metric) can predict patients benefiting from DA-VMAT.</jats:p>

                    <jats:title>Methods:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Forty-five patients with localised prostate cancer (cT1–T2, N0, M0) were retrospectively analysed. SA and DA-VMAT plans (78 Gy/39 fractions) were generated using Monaco. Comparisons included dose-volume histogram (DVH) metrics, homogeneity and conformity indices, gEUD, TCP and NTCP. Plan deliverability was assessed using monitor units (MUs), beam-on time, modulation complexity score (MCSv) and gamma analysis. The Mq,r index (PTV–OAR spatial relationship) and F metric (anatomical confinement) were analysed for correlation with DA benefit and predictive ability using ROC analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="S1460396926100727_as3">
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Target coverage was comparable between the two techniques (PTV D95%: 74·2 vs 74·5 Gy,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      = 0·21). DA-VMAT improved homogeneity (p = 0·03) and reduced the rectal dose (V40Gy: 35·2% vs. 38·1%; V65Gy: 18·4% vs. 21·3%), resulting in a modest NTCP reduction (4·8% vs. 3·9%). However, DA-VMAT increased the MUs (542 vs. 426), beam-on time (152 vs. 118 s) and complexity (MCSv: 0·72 vs. 0·84; all
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      < 0·01). Both Mq,r and F correlated with NTCP reduction (

                    <jats:title>Conclusion:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>DA-VMAT provides modest improvements in rectal sparing and homogeneity but increases complexity and treatment time. Anatomy-based metrics may support personalised arc selection and warrant prospective validation.</jats:p>

title: Paediatric radiotherapy in Denmark from 2008 to 2024: implementation of improved radiotherapeutic technologies
items.abstract:
<jats:p>Introduction: Modern radiotherapy technologies are essential for reducing treatment-related morbidity and late effects. However, their implementation in paediatric oncology often lags behind adult practice despite their potential to improve survivorship. This study aims to characterise the nationwide use of radiotherapy technologies in Danish paediatric cancer care from 2008 to 2024.
Methods: Data were obtained from the radiotherapy sub-registry of the Danish Childhood Cancer Registry and included all Danish patients diagnosed before age 18 who received radiotherapy between 2008 and 2024. Data collected comprised treatment modality, image guidance, motion management, fractionation, and dose.
Results: A total of 651 patients received radiotherapy, including 109 who underwent a second course of treatment. Overall, 243 treatments were proton-based and 458 photon-based. The use of volumetric modulated arc therapy and proton therapy increased over time, although adoption varied by diagnosis, e.g., conformal techniques were introduced later for Wilms tumour. Daily image-guided radiotherapy became standard practice from the late 2010s, with cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) largely replacing other imaging modalities, particularly for soft-tissue and abdominal targets. Deep inspiration breath-hold was initially limited to lymphoma patients but expanded to other diagnoses and younger age groups after 2017.
Conclusion: This nationwide study documents the technological evolution of paediatric radiotherapy in Denmark over a 16-year period. State-of-the-art conformal techniques were broadly implemented, although the pace of adoption varied across diagnoses, likely reflecting protocol requirements and clinical caution. The findings suggest that clinical trials are important drivers of technological innovation and highlight the importance of monitoring implementation to ensure that advances in radiotherapy translate into paediatric radiotherapy.</jats:p>

                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To develop and internally validate a machine learning-based predictive model for radiation dermatitis (RD) in cervical cancer patients undergoing radiotherapy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 251 cervical cancer patients receiving pelvic external beam radiotherapy were prospectively enrolled and randomly divided into a training set and a validation set at a 7:3 ratio. In the training set, LASSO regression was used to select predictors, and four models—logistic regression (LR), random forest (RF), support vector machine (SVM), and XGBoost—were constructed. Hyperparameter tuning was performed using grid search, model stability was assessed via 5-fold cross-validation, and DeLong tests were used to compare AUC differences among models. Model performance was evaluated in the validation set using AUC, sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, precision, and F1 score. Calibration of the optimal model was assessed using calibration curves, the Hosmer-Lemeshow test, and the Brier score.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>LASSO regression identified five predictors: age, immobilizer type, total dose, hypertension, and PNI. In the validation set, the LR model achieved an AUC of 0.810, sensitivity of 0.780, specificity of 0.760, accuracy of 0.773, and F1 score of 0.821; the AUCs for RF, SVM, and XGBoost were 0.854, 0.777, and 0.766, respectively. Overall, the LR model demonstrated excellent specificity comparable to the best-performing model, with good discrimination and calibration in the internal validation cohort, and was therefore selected as the optimal model. The calibration curve showed good agreement between predicted and observed probabilities, with a Hosmer-Lemeshow test P = 0.080 and a Brier score of 0.168.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The LR model based on age, immobilizer type, total dose, hypertension, and PNI demonstrates good predictive performance for RD in cervical cancer patients receiving radiotherapy. As an internally validated model with readily available predictors, it holds potential to assist in early identification of patients at high risk for RD, providing a reference for individualized nursing care and preventive interventions.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>The paper presents a calculation-experimental method for improving the endurance of a multirotor UAV using a custom 10-inch FPV platform as a case study. The proposed approach considers the UAV not as a set of separate components but as an integrated energy-conversion system that includes a Li-ion battery, ESCs, BLDC motors, propellers, frame layout and mass distribution. A key design constraint is the propeller tip Mach number, since approaching the transonic region increases noise, vibration and aerodynamic losses. For the tested platform equipped with 3115 900KV motors and 10-inch propellers, a 6S3P Li-ion battery pack with a capacity of 15 Ah and a mass of 1.3 kg was selected. Flight tests demonstrated 52 min of hovering without payload and 37.5 min with a 0.657 kg payload. The specific efficiency was 8.1 g/W and 6.4 g/W, respectively. The results confirm that endurance improvement requires coordinated matching of the motor KV, battery voltage, propeller diameter, take-off mass and mechanical layout.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Layered transition metal dichalcogenides can reversibly accommodate different alkali ions, yet their transport kinetics depend strongly on alkali identity and the associated structural evolution. CrSe2 can host one Li or Na ion per formula unit, but their relative kinetic accessibility during electrochemical intercalation and deintercalation and chemical deintercalation has not been established. Here, we use an optimized route to prepare O1−LiCrSe2 and O3−NaCrSe2 for a matched Li−Na kinetic comparison. Operando diffraction and composition-resolved chemical deintercalation distinguish an O1-retaining Li pathway from an O1/O3 structural transformation for Na. At 1 C, CrSe2||Li and CrSe2||Na delivers comparable capacities of 127 and 128 mAh g−1, respectively. At 25 C, CrSe2||Na retains 70% of its 1 C capacity, corresponding to 89 mAh g−1, whereas CrSe2||Li retains 55%, corresponding to 70 mAh g−1. Under the same chemical-deintercalation protocol, the iodine-consumption endpoint for the nominal alkali-free composition is reached after 8.1 h for NaCrSe2 and 26.9 h for LiCrSe2, respectively. The lower electrochemical polarization and calculated migration barrier for Na in NaCrSe2, 0.41 eV compared with 0.48 eV for Li in LiCrSe2, further support this kinetic ordering. These results establish greater kinetic accessibility for Na than Li within the layered CrSe2 framework despite the more extensive structural rearrangement associated with Na transport.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Colloidal quantum dots (QDs) are attractive nanoscale emitters, yet their response to energetic electron excitation remains poorly understood and often unstable, limiting cathodoluminescence (CL) spectroscopy, radiation‐detection applications, and electron‐beam‐based device processing. Here, we investigate the CL response of giant‐shell CdSe/CdS QDs and strategies to improve its stability through combined in situ CL and photoluminescence (PL) measurements. Spectral and lifetime analysis reveals efficient multiexciton excitation, leading to blueshifted emission and faster dynamics, while charge accumulation contributes to cathodobleaching. Using indirect excitation to reach sub‐pA effective currents, we demonstrate partial recovery of long‐lived neutral‐exciton emission and strongly reduced cathodobleaching, although biexciton emission persists even at these low currents. Furthermore, replacing long insulating ligands with shorter ones strongly suppresses biexciton emission, consistent with improved charge drainage. Our work presents two complementary methods to control the CL response of QDs under electron‐beam excitation, providing a practical route toward stable CL for spectroscopy and imaging, fast scintillation, and electron‐beam‐compatible photonic devices.</jats:p>

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Radiotherapy is an essential component of comprehensive treatment for breast cancer. While improving therapeutic efficacy, it also causes various adverse effects and compromises patients’ quality of life, especially during the vulnerable early post-radiotherapy period. Exploring breast cancer survivors’ real rehabilitation experiences is critical to supporting their full recovery after radiotherapy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Based on the Breast Cancer Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement System (PROMS-B), a validated framework for assessing cancer survivors’ holistic health, this study explored physical, psychological, and social experiences during the first 3 months after radiotherapy completion, to inform the optimization of nursing interventions and follow-up strategies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Purposive sampling was used to recruit 28 breast cancer survivors from a tertiary hospital in Ningxia between October 2025 and January 2026. Data were collected via semi-structured interviews and analyzed using conventional content analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Four main themes with 11 sub-themes emerged: 1) Physical health: prevalent skin reactions and fatigue with limited proactive self-management; 2) Psychological health: common body image disturbance and negative emotions, with partial active adjustment; 3) Social health: weakened social roles, financial pressure, and mixed impacts of social support; 4) Rehabilitation needs: prominent information gaps and strong demand for exercise and prognosis guidance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study highlights the multifaceted and interconnected challenges faced by breast cancer survivors during the high-risk early post-radiotherapy period. The findings support the development of a nurse-led, holistic transitional care model including stepwise skill-based education provided at radiotherapy completion, accessible digital psychological support, integrated hospital-community-family networks, and structured proactive follow-up. These strategies may improve self-management ability, relieve symptom burden, and promote successful social reintegration and long-term rehabilitation among breast cancer survivors.</jats:p>

                    <jats:p>Heart and lung exposure are often discussed together in breast radiotherapy, although their doses may arise from different constraints. We tested whether contemporary breast radiotherapy is characterized by organ-specific dose-generating mechanisms rather than a common determinant structure.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This retrospective study included 276 women with unilateral breast cancer treated with intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) or volumetric-modulated arc therapy (VMAT) from January 2022 through June 2023. Mean heart dose (Heart Dmean) and ipsilateral lung mean dose (Lung Dmean) were modeled using multivariable ordinary least-squares regression with HC3 robust standard errors. Four-degree-of-freedom B-splines assessed nonlinear planning-target-volume (PTV) effects. Organ-by-factor interactions were examined in a joint standardized mixed model. Maximum heart distance (MHD) was evaluated in left-sided cases. Sensitivity analyses included Gamma generalized linear models and exclusion of deep-inspiration breath-hold cases. Exploratory Shapley/LMG decomposition quantified each predictor group’s share of model-explained variance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Left-sided disease was the dominant determinant of Heart Dmean (+217.38 cGy; 95% CI, 184.59–250.18; P&lt;.001), whereas regional nodal irradiation (RNI) was the strongest determinant of Lung Dmean (+271.30 cGy; 95% CI, 182.52–360.07; P&lt;.001). PTV volume showed a nonlinear association with Lung Dmean (joint spline P&lt;.001) but not Heart Dmean (P = .119). VMAT was associated with lower Lung Dmean (−93.05 cGy; P = .011) without a corresponding Heart Dmean difference. The joint model confirmed organ-specific effects for laterality, RNI, and technique. Among 128 left-sided patients, MHD was not associated with Heart Dmean (Spearman ρ=.071; P = .424). Shapley/LMG decomposition attributed 81.9% of explained Heart Dmean variance to laterality, whereas RNI contributed the largest share for Lung Dmean (35.4%).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cardiac and ipsilateral lung dose followed different constraint hierarchies: anatomy dominated cardiac exposure, while treatment extent and target geometry dominated lung exposure. Organ-specific models may therefore be more useful than generic normal-tissue risk frameworks for individualized breast radiotherapy planning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Geometric calibration of a four-channel plane-mirror interferometer requires separating translation–yaw coupling from beam-pointing and mirror-orientation effects. This numerical study examines paired ranges acquired at matched positions with nonzero and zero yaw. A scaled analytic Jacobian identifies weak parameter combinations, and an equal-budget search compares 70 four-level yaw sets. The eight-parameter model has full local numerical rank but a condition number of 9.42×105. Fixing two mirror angles at their synthetic truth reduces the condition number to 2519. The selected yaw levels are {−2.4,−1.8,1.8,2.4} mrad. Four solver configurations are compared over 100 synthetic recalibrations. Their similar held-out residuals conceal differences in parameter recovery: an additive decomposition assigns 3.67 nm RMS to yaw-reference mismatch within a 3.70 nm total residual. Controlled noise/yaw switches further separate calibration-induced parameter error from validation-side mismatch. These results identify survey and angular-reference requirements for the declared geometry and provide a local numerical design screen; physical accuracy remains to be established experimentally.</jats:p>

title: Safety, accuracy, empathy, and readability of four large language models answering esophageal cancer radiotherapy adverse-effect questions: a comparative study
